newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs give Moslems ultimatum to quit village.
newsitem.headline: Serbs give Moslems ultimatum to quit village.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities gave a group of Moslems who returned to their home village in eastern Bosnia an ultimatum to leave or be thrown out but have extended a deadline to Wednesday, NATO sources said on Monday.
A NATO peace force (IFOR) spokesman said earlier that it knew nothing about an ultimatum with a Monday 1500 GMT deadline mentioned by Serb interior minister Dragan Kijac to Reuters.

But an IFOR source who asked for anonymity said later that U.N. police commissioner Peter Fitzgerald was meeting with Kijac and added: "Kijac is being reasonable. We understand he's given another 48 hours before police do anything."
NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock said: "We have assurances from the Serb republic police they will do nothing precipitous and keep us informed what they want to do".

Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the International Police Task Force in postwar Bosnia, confirmed the Serbs had earlier set a 1500 GMT Monday deadline after allowing an initial 1000 GMT time limit to lapse without action.
IFOR reported on Sunday that a group of about 100 Moslems carrying banned weapons moved into the ruined village in Serb- held territory in eastern Bosnia over the weekend.
Major Brett Boudreau, another IFOR spokesman, said the Dayton peace agreement ensures the right of war refugees to return to their homes but under safe conditions only.
Moving refugees back to sensitive areas near former front lines required a patient, "phased approach" which should be coordinated with refugee agencies, he said.
NATO sources, who asked not to be identified, said moving in an armed group of Moslem military-age men into the zone of separation was clearly "provocative".

The village, almost totally destroyed during the Bosnian war, lies in the "zone of separation" near former front lines where submachine guns and other weapons are banned under terms of the Dayton peace agreement.
"They are military age men and they are bringing in weapons with them," Boudreau told Reuters. "At this stage it seems a little too coincidental."
He said the situation was a "carbon copy" of events last month in the nearby village of Mahala.
A similar incident last month led to a violence when Moslem men entered Mahala and Serb police armed with pistols and clubs attacked them. Moslems. IFOR ultimately blamed both sides.
Before May 27, 1992 Jusici was a Moslem village with some 140 houses. After that day it was a burnt-out wreck.

"I was working in the field on May 27 ... nobody suspected anything," says Fatija Ibrahimovic, 51. "All of a sudden, it was around eleven, Serb forces - army, paramilitary and our neighbours - were all around us.
"They forced us, women and children, into the school building, and then massacred most of the men," she added.
"I came back because I want to die in my house, now that I wasn't given a chance to live a decent life in it".
Ibrahimovic is one of 150 Moslem refugees have now moved back to Jusici, near Zvornik, after living mainly in Moslem-controlled Tuzla since 1992.
Her house was flattened by explosives just like many others in the area.
"They took away my husband, my brother and his son. I still have no idea what happened to them, but I presume they must be dead," she said.
But Ibrahimovic is determined to stay in her home no matter what: "I'll stay here even if it means getting killed. My soul is dead anyway."
Serbs living in a nearby village are furious at the very notion the Moslems might return.

"This is our land, they can't come back. Why did we ever fight this war in the first place?" said Milan Zerkovic, 47, in Malesici, the nearest village to Jusici just a one km (half a mile) to the south.
"If our authorities or the international community do not make them leave, rest assured that we will!" he said.
"My son died in this war and God help me if I let my daughter live anywhere near them again," his wife Ljubinka said.
